results.result: The authors collected a complete serial-section EM dataset spanning the entire CNS of a single Ciona larva, comprising 6,928 sections at varying thicknesses (60-100 nm) and imaged at 3.85 nm/pixel resolution. This dataset captured 301 CNS cells including 177 neurons.
results.evaluation: The methodological claims are well-documented with specific section counts and imaging parameters. The completeness is verified by the ability to trace all neurons and their connections. However, the study is limited to a single individual, which is acknowledged but limits generalizability.

results.result: The connectome comprises 177 CNS neurons forming 6,618 chemical synapses (>1 section) including 1,772 neuromuscular junctions, and 1,206 gap junctions (>1 section). Each neuron forms an average of 49 presynaptic sites and 13 gap junctions, receiving an average of 39 synapses from presynaptic partners.
results.evaluation: These quantitative measures are directly derived from the EM reconstruction with clear counting criteria. The statistics (means, standard deviations, ranges) are appropriately reported. The distinction between total contacts and those spanning >1 section provides quality control.

results.result: Ciona CNS neurons exhibit distinctive structural features: unipolar morphology with at most a single dendrite, predominance of axo-axonal synapses (68% of neuron-neuron synapses terminate on axons/terminals), presence of ciliary organelles in most neurons, and 922 polyadic synapses (10.7% of total).
results.evaluation: These morphological characterizations are well-supported by EM observations and quantification. The predominance of axo-axonal synapses is unusual compared to vertebrate systems and is quantitatively documented. The ciliary organelles are a notable feature confirmed by direct observation.

results.result: Synapses in Ciona exhibit diverse vesicle populations including small electron-lucent vesicles (30-60 nm), larger electron-lucent vesicles (70-110 nm), and dense-core vesicles of varying sizes (40-140 nm). Postsynaptic densities are present at some but not all synapses, making them unreliable identification criteria. Gap junctions were identified by membrane densities on both sides.
results.evaluation: The vesicle characterization is based on direct EM observation with size measurements. The acknowledgment that postsynaptic densities are unreliable is methodologically important and honest. The gap junction identification criteria follow established standards (Bennett and Goodenough, 1978).

results.result: Network analysis reveals that presynaptic site number varies with postsynaptic partner number, weak correlation between axon/terminal surface area and synapse number (r²=0.7), but no correlation between soma volume and synapse number (r²=0.4). The network forms a single connected component with characteristic path length of 2.7, average of 20 synaptic partners per neuron, and clustering coefficient of 0.333.
results.evaluation: The network statistics are appropriately calculated and reported. The correlation analyses are valid, though the r² values indicate substantial unexplained variance. The single connected component is an important finding. However, the biological interpretation of these network metrics could be more developed.

results.result: Despite nearly equal total cell numbers on left and right sides (left: 125; right: 129; midline: 46), the brain vesicle shows asymmetric distribution of cell types with more sensory neurons and pigment cells on the right (including the right-sided ocellus) and more interneurons on the left (including 17 left-sided coronet cells). The motor ganglion shows asymmetries in ACIN numbers (2 left, 1 right) and presence of 2 PMGNs only on the right.
results.evaluation: The cellular asymmetries are well-documented through complete reconstruction. The reclassification of some ependymal cells as neurons based on EM data (C75) strengthens the findings. However, the functional significance of these asymmetries requires further investigation. The single-larva limitation is important here.

results.result: The left side contains 17 coronet cells with dopamine immunoreactivity, short axons terminating at the basal lamina with dense-core vesicles (80-110 nm). The right side contains 30 photoreceptors (23 with outer segments in ocellus pigment, 7 in neural canal) arranged in five rows, plus 7 additional Group III photoreceptors and 3 anterior sensory interneurons.
results.evaluation: The sensory neuron characterization combines EM reconstruction with prior immunolabeling data (Horie et al., 2008; Moret et al., 2005). The photoreceptor counts reconcile previous discrepancies in the literature. The structural descriptions are detailed and well-supported by the EM data.

results.result: Sensory pathways show pronounced asymmetry: Type II canal photoreceptors connect only to right-side pr-AMG relay neurons, while left-side PRRN relay neurons receive input exclusively from Type I ocellus photoreceptors. Antenna cell 1 projects bilaterally while antenna cell 2 projects predominantly to right-side relay neurons. Relay neurons project asymmetrically to the motor ganglion (photoreceptor interneurons 70% to left, antenna interneurons 70% to right).
results.evaluation: The asymmetric connectivity patterns are quantitatively documented and represent a major finding. The 70% asymmetry in relay neuron projections is substantial and well-characterized. However, the functional consequences for behavior are speculative and require experimental validation.

results.result: Motor neurons show differential neuromuscular junction characteristics: MN1 and MN2 form 200-360 large synapses with clear postsynaptic densities, while MN3-MN5 form 15-50 smaller junctions. Neuromuscular input is asymmetric for all motor neuron pairs except MN2 (which shows 46:54 left:right symmetry), with asymmetries falling within 60:40 to 40:60 ratios. Motor neurons also form asymmetric synapses with each other.
results.evaluation: The motor neuron characterization is detailed and quantitative. The distinction between primary (MN1-2) and secondary (MN3-5) motor neurons is well-supported. The asymmetries are modest but consistent. The functional significance of these asymmetries for swimming behavior requires experimental testing.

results.result: Motor ganglion interneuron networks show pronounced asymmetries: synaptic strength from MGIN1 to MGIN2 is far greater on the left side, paralleled by gap junction connections only on the left between MGIN2L and MGIN1L. MGIN2L also connects to contralateral MGIN1R via gap junctions. MN1 receives stronger input from MGIN1 and MGIN3 on the right (1.08 and 1.2 μm vs 0.42 and 0.72 μm), and MN2 receives stronger input from MGIN2R than MGIN2L (4.69 vs 1.24 μm).
results.evaluation: The interneuron asymmetries are quantified using synaptic depth as a proxy for strength. The parallel asymmetries in chemical and electrical synapses strengthen the findings. However, synaptic depth may not perfectly correlate with functional strength, and physiological validation would be valuable.

results.result: ACINs show striking asymmetries in number (2 left, 1 right), projections (left ACINs fully decussate and form contralateral synapses; right ACIN crosses midline but forms no contralateral synapses), and targets (contralateral synapses target interneurons MGIN1R, MGIN2R, MGIN3R, not motor neurons directly as previously proposed). All ACINs are presynaptic to ipsilateral motor neurons, right-side bipolar tail neuron BTN2, and the ventral basal lamina. Presynaptic inputs differ among the three ACINs.
results.evaluation: The ACIN asymmetries are among the most striking findings and directly contradict previous models (Horie et al., 2010). The complete reconstruction provides definitive evidence for the connectivity patterns. The failure of the right ACIN to extend into left neuropil despite crossing the midline is particularly notable. This result challenges existing CPG models.

results.result: The connectivity matrix reveals several organizational principles: most cell types form synapses among members of the same class; many synapses form on basal lamina and from motor neurons to muscle; high reciprocity between different neuron classes, especially interneurons; neurons with many presynaptic sites generally have many postsynaptic sites (except sensory neurons); pathway strength is greater in motor ganglion and among relay neurons; cell classes with fewer neurons tend to have greater pathway strengths.
results.evaluation: These network organizational principles are derived from systematic analysis of the complete connectivity matrix. The observations are well-supported, though some (like the relationship between cell class size and pathway strength) could benefit from statistical testing. The high reciprocity is notable and quantified.

results.result: The complete synaptic connectome reveals that despite shared evolutionary ancestry with chordates, the Ciona larval CNS incorporates many pathways that are manifestly left-right asymmetrical, contrasting with bilaterally symmetrical pathways reported in vertebrate brains. These asymmetries are interpreted as an ascidian specialization resulting from small cell numbers and rapid development, compatible with the larva's sensorimotor behavior and helical swimming pattern.
results.evaluation: While the asymmetries are well-documented, the interpretation as an ascidian specialization is speculative. The comparison to vertebrate brains may be premature, as detailed connectomes at this resolution are not available for vertebrates. The link to helical swimming is plausible but not experimentally demonstrated. The single-larva limitation is critical for this broad conclusion.

results.result: The authors note that symmetry-based validation approaches used in other connectome studies could not be applied in Ciona due to lack of bilateral pairing in the brain vesicle and asymmetrical inputs to paired motor ganglion neurons. They acknowledge that minor asymmetries might result from developmental noise or imprecision.
results.evaluation: This is an honest acknowledgment of methodological limitations and uncertainty. The inability to use symmetry for validation is a significant limitation that increases the importance of the single-larva caveat. The developmental noise possibility is appropriately raised but cannot be distinguished from functional asymmetry without additional specimens.

results.result: Brain asymmetry development requires Nodal expression and ciliary action during embryonic development, processes perturbed by dechorionation used in many experimental interventions. The embryo curls along the left side within the chorion, potentially influencing brain sidedness. Dechorionation significantly alters arrestin expression, often expanding photoreceptor fate to the left brain.
results.evaluation: These claims are well-supported by cited literature (Nishide et al., 2012; Thompson et al., 2012; Shimeld and Levin, 2006; Katsumoto et al., 2013; Oonuma et al., 2016). This provides important context for why asymmetries may have been missed in previous studies and validates the authors' approach of using chorion-intact larvae.

results.result: The larval ascidian CNS asymmetries show parallels with other chordates including vertebrates (but differ from other deuterostomes like echinoderms). The ocellus pigment migration driven by Nodal is compared to vertebrate pineal lateralization, though pigment cells migrate right in Ciona versus left in vertebrates. Ciona's eyes are more akin to lateral eyes than pineal based on outer segment projection. Coronet cells are proposed as homologous to the bilateral vertebrate saccus vasculosus, with ciliated coronet-associated neurons giving rise to axonal pathways in both cases.
results.evaluation: The evolutionary comparisons are interesting but speculative. The homology between coronet cells and saccus vasculosus is based on morphological similarity and requires molecular/developmental validation. The comparison to vertebrate pineal is complicated by opposite migration directions. The interpretation that Ciona eyes are lateral rather than pineal-like is reasonable but not definitive.

results.result: Given helical swimming and single-sided ocellus, Ciona larvae follow helical rather than visual phototaxis. However, the complement of cell types and circuit complexity more closely resembles visual phototaxis circuits than simple helical phototaxis. Helical swimming may represent a mechanism by which a preexisting bilateral visual phototaxis circuit was co-opted into a complex hybrid helical phototaxis circuit.
results.evaluation: This evolutionary hypothesis is creative but speculative. The circuit complexity comparison to other organisms (Randel and Jékely, 2016) is interesting but the functional classification requires behavioral experiments. The co-option hypothesis is plausible but lacks direct evidence. This represents an interesting direction for future work rather than a supported conclusion.

results.result: Unilateral systems in Ciona that show homology with bilateral vertebrate structures are interpreted as reduction in one side due to miniaturization. The larva's small cell numbers result from few embryonic cleavages (≤14 for entire CNS), lack of metamerism, lack of feeding, and short life. Despite small neuron numbers (177 vs 302 in C. elegans), Ciona shows rich cell type diversity with 25 types and 52 subtypes, comparable to C. elegans' 118 types among 302 neurons.
results.evaluation: The miniaturization interpretation is reasonable and well-contextualized with developmental data. The cell type richness despite small neuron numbers is well-documented and represents an important finding. The comparison to C. elegans is appropriate and highlights that cell type diversity can be maintained despite small total neuron numbers.

results.result: Asymmetries begin appearing at ~75% of embryonic development with failure of cells to pair left/right, followed by brain vesicle pushing right (75-85% development). Cell lineage is left/right symmetrical until 11th cleavage, with photoreceptor pigment cell migration and ACIN appearance after this point. Total cell numbers remain mostly symmetrical, with sidedness primarily reflecting cell fate decisions (neuron vs ependymal). ACIN number variation between larvae (Nishino et al., 2010) manifests as asymmetry in this larva (2 left, 1 right), proposed to result from variable cell fate decisions.
results.evaluation: The developmental timeline is well-supported by cited literature (Cole and Meinertzhagen, 2004; Nishitsuji et al., 2012). The interpretation that asymmetry primarily reflects cell fate rather than cell number is insightful and well-argued. The ACIN asymmetry explanation is plausible but would benefit from examination of additional larvae to confirm the variability pattern.

results.result: The conclusions are based on a single larva, though four unrelated sibling larvae have been reported with closely similar overall cell complements (Nicol and Meinertzhagen, 1991).
results.evaluation: This is an honest and critical acknowledgment of the study's primary limitation. The citation of previous work showing consistency in cell complements provides some support for generalizability, but the lack of connectome data from multiple individuals remains a significant limitation for all conclusions, especially regarding asymmetries that might vary between individuals.

results.result: The previously proposed CPG model for Ciona (Horie et al., 2010) is left-right symmetrical with direct contralateral input to motor neurons, features now shown to be lacking in the actual connectome. The left-right difference in ACIN connections is particularly surprising, with the right ACIN failing to extend into left neuropil despite crossing the midline.
results.evaluation: This represents an important correction to the literature. The connectome data definitively shows that the previous CPG model was incorrect regarding symmetry and ACIN connectivity. This highlights the value of complete connectome reconstruction over inference from partial data. However, the functional implications require experimental validation.

results.result: Larvae swim in a helical pattern from bilateral tail flexions. The helical pattern may reflect motor pathway asymmetry, though varying light direction could also generate helical klinotaxis. Based on gravitaxis in young larvae, antenna neuron circuits are predicted to underlie directional gravity response. Asymmetries in sensory input to the motor ganglion suggest sensory input should generate sided swimming movements on a fixed side of each animal, as video recordings suggest.
results.evaluation: These functional predictions are reasonable based on the connectome data but remain speculative without experimental validation. The video evidence (Videos 7-8) is suggestive but not rigorously quantified. The multiple possible mechanisms for helical swimming (pathway asymmetry vs. klinotaxis) cannot be distinguished without perturbation experiments. These represent testable hypotheses rather than supported conclusions.

results.result: Unpolarized synapses have been previously reported in coelenterates and pulmonate molluscs, while synapses onto basal lamina have been reported in muscle after myofibre removal. Synaptic reciprocity and serial networks are commonplace in many nervous systems.
results.evaluation: These comparative claims are well-supported by appropriate citations (Horridge and Mackay, 1962; McCarrager and Chase, 1985; Sanes et al., 1978; Dowling and Boycott, 1966). They provide useful context for interpreting the unusual features observed in Ciona as not entirely unique but part of broader patterns in nervous system organization.

results.result: Ciona's 177 CNS neurons with average 37 presynaptic sites and 7 gap junctions are numerically comparable to C. elegans (302 neurons, 28 synapses and 3.2 gap junctions per neuron), smaller than Drosophila optic lobe neurons (>100 presynaptic sites), and much smaller than vertebrate neurons (e.g., mouse cortex neuron ~8200 synapses).
results.evaluation: These comparative statistics are appropriately calculated and cited. They provide useful context for understanding Ciona's nervous system complexity relative to other model organisms. The comparisons are fair and highlight that Ciona represents an intermediate level of synaptic complexity.
